title: Value Filling Over a Quarter
statement:
You get an integer array arr sorted in non-decreasing order. Exactly one value occurs more than arr.length / 4 times. Return that value.

"More than a quarter" is strict: a value that fills exactly 25% of the array does not count.

examples.why: 2 occurs 3 times, and 3 > 10 / 4 = 2.5. The middle element arr[5] is 4, so "take the middle" fails here.
1 occurs 2 times, which is exactly 8 / 4 and so not enough. 4 occurs 3 times.
The only value fills the whole array.

constraints: arr is sorted in non-decreasing order
Exactly one value occurs more than arr.length / 4 times
hints: Counting each run in one pass works in O(n). The array is sorted, so what does a long run of one value look like in index terms?
If a value fills more than n/4 slots, then arr[i] === arr[i + ⌊n/4⌋] for its first index i. Also, its run must cover at least one of the positions ⌊n/4⌋, ⌊n/2⌋, ⌊3n/4⌋.
Take each of those three positions as a candidate, binary search its first and last occurrence, and return the candidate whose run is longer than n/4.

explain.intuition:
Split the array into four quarters. A run longer than a quarter of the array cannot fit between two quarter marks without touching one of them. So the answer must sit at index ⌊n/4⌋, ⌊n/2⌋ or ⌊3n/4⌋. That leaves only three candidates.

Because the array is sorted, all copies of a value form one block. Binary search for the block's first and last index (lower and upper bound) gives its length in O(log n). Check the three candidates and return the one whose block is longer than n / 4.
steps: For each candidate index c in ⌊n/4⌋, ⌊n/2⌋, ⌊3n/4⌋, let v = arr[c].
Binary search the first index lo with arr[lo] ≥ v and the first index hi with arr[hi] > v.
The guarantee means one of the three always succeeds.
pitfalls: Using ≥ instead of >. A value filling exactly 25% would be returned too early, like the 1 in the second example.
Returning the middle element. A block longer than a quarter does not have to reach the middle.
Comparing count > n / 4 with integer division in a typed language: for n = 10 that is 2, and a count of 3 still passes, but a count of exactly n/4 must not. Multiply instead: 4 · count > n.

solutions.title: Count every value by scanning
solutions.idea: For each position, count how often its value occurs in the whole array.

solutions.title: Compare with the element a quarter ahead
solutions.idea: A block longer than n/4 starting at i still holds the same value at i + ⌊n/4⌋. A shorter block never does.

solutions.title: Binary search at the quarter marks
solutions.idea: The answer's block must cover index n/4, n/2 or 3n/4. Measure each candidate's block with two binary searches.

followups: Find every value that occurs more than n/k times, for a given k. How many candidates are there?
The array is not sorted. Can you still find a value occurring more than n/4 times in O(n) time and O(1) space?
